title: Phaethon and the Chariot of the Sun
text:
Phaethon's mother had told him that his father was the Sun. When a friend mocked him for believing it, Phaethon traveled to the far east to the Sun's palace to find out for himself.

His father welcomed him, took off his blazing crown so the boy could come close, and confirmed that he was his son. To prove it, he swore by the river Styx, an oath the gods cannot break, to grant Phaethon any wish.

Phaethon asked to drive the chariot of the Sun across the sky for one day. His father regretted his promise at once. Not even Jupiter could drive those horses, he said. He begged his son to choose anything else. But Phaethon insisted, and the oath held.

The fiery horses felt the light weight in the chariot and ran wild. They left their road, plunged near the earth and scorched it: mountains burned, rivers boiled away, cities and peoples turned to ash. The Earth herself cried out to Jupiter. To save the world, he struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt. The boy fell blazing like a falling star into the river Eridanus. His sisters wept over his grave until they were turned into poplar trees, their tears hardening into amber.
lesson: Love that tries to prove itself by granting anything can do great harm. A parent's real gift is sometimes the refusal.
location: Greek myth; written in Rome, Italy
